h1: Trivandrum SEO: Technopark software and Ayurveda both
metaTitle: SEO Company in Thiruvananthapuram: Tech and Ayurveda
metaDescription: Trivandrum sells software to the US and Ayurveda to Europe. Two audiences, two keyword sets, one retainer, and a 90-day guarantee on your own baseline.
answer: Thiruvananthapuram runs two export businesses that search in opposite directions: Technopark software firms chasing US and European B2B buyers, and Ayurveda centres chasing European wellness travellers. They need different keyword sets, different content and different seasons, so we scope and price them as two separate campaigns even inside one retainer.
takeaways: A Technopark firm and an Ayurveda resort share a pin code and nothing else in search. Never run one playbook across both.
Ayurveda's domestic peak is the Karkidakam monsoon window. Its European peak is the dry season. Publish six months ahead of whichever you sell to.
Health claims are legally constrained in India. The 1954 Drugs and Magic Remedies Act is not optional, and it shapes what your pages can say.
Malayalam matters for the clinic-school-retail layer of the city and barely at all for the export layer.

sections.h2: Two export businesses, two entirely different search markets
body: Technopark opened in 1990 as India's first IT park, and the campus plus its satellite offices now anchor a services economy that sells almost entirely outside India. In the same city, a wellness industry sells Ayurveda to Germans, Russians, Israelis and Gulf visitors who arrive for two to four weeks at a time.
Both are export businesses. Both are searched for in English. Everything else about them is different — the buyer, the query shape, the sales cycle, the season, and what counts as proof.

sections.h2: Technopark firms and the query set that actually gets an RFP
body: The trap for a Kerala IT services company is ranking for "software development company in Trivandrum". It's easy, it feels like progress, and the people typing it are mostly job seekers and local vendors.

Buyers in Boston and Berlin type something else entirely. They type the technology, the platform, the compliance regime and the engagement model. Their searches read like a requirements document: the framework plus the industry, the ERP plus "implementation partner", the standard plus "certified development team", "offshore" or "nearshore" plus the discipline.

That's a competitive national and international keyword set, and winning it needs three things most Technopark sites don't have: technical depth published under a named engineer's byline, a security and compliance page that survives a vendor questionnaire, and case content specific enough to be useful without breaching an NDA. If you can't name the client, name the problem, the constraint and the measurable outcome. Buyers read for the constraint.

We run these as international campaigns from a Kerala base — see [what the SEO retainer covers](/seo) — and they are priced like international campaigns, because the competition is Poland and Vietnam, not the next block in Kazhakkoottam.

sections.h2: Ayurveda, wellness travel and the calendar you actually sell into
body: Kerala Ayurveda has something most wellness markets would pay for: genuine provenance, a regulated classification, and a body of treatment tradition that people travel a continent for. Kerala Tourism's Green Leaf and Olive Leaf classification for Ayurveda centres is a real, verifiable signal — and most classified centres barely mention it on their site, which is a wasted trust asset and a wasted keyword.

Then there's the season problem, which is the single most common reason a Trivandrum wellness site under-performs. The domestic market peaks in Karkidakam, the monsoon month roughly mid-July to mid-August, when monsoon treatment is traditional. The European inbound market runs almost the opposite way, weighted towards the drier months from around October to March.

Those are two different content calendars. Pages ranking for a season you sell into have to be published and indexed months before it, because search demand for a three-week retreat builds long before the booking. If you publish your monsoon-therapy page in July, you've published it for next year.
bullets: Write for the condition and the duration, not the brochure. "14 day panchakarma" and "Ayurvedic treatment for chronic back pain" are how people search.
Publish the practical logistics European travellers actually check: visa type, airport transfer, single-occupancy pricing, diet, what a treatment day looks like, what you can and can't do afterwards.
Name your physicians with their BAMS or MD (Ay) qualification and registration. Anonymous "expert doctors" is the weakest possible signal in a category built on trust.
Reviews in the traveller's own language carry disproportionate weight. Ask for them in German or Russian if that's who you serve.

sections.h2: Medical value travel, and the law that limits what you can say
body: India actively courts medical value travel, including a dedicated visa category for treatment and for Ayush. That's a genuine tailwind for Trivandrum, and it's why hospital and wellness marketing here keeps drifting towards claims it isn't allowed to make.

The Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act, 1954 restricts advertising that claims to diagnose, cure or prevent the conditions listed in its schedule. The advertising self-regulation code adds its own constraints, medical council rules limit how registered practitioners may advertise, and consumer protection law covers misleading claims generally. None of this is exotic — it's the baseline any competent healthcare marketer works inside.

The practical effect on SEO is useful rather than limiting. You cannot promise a cure, so you compete on something harder to fake: process transparency, physician credentials, facility detail, honest treatment durations, realistic expectations, and post-treatment guidance. That is also, coincidentally, exactly the content that earns links and survives a Google medical-content update.
If you sell treatment, have your copy reviewed by someone who knows this law before it goes live. A page pulled after it ranks costs more than one that ranked slower.

callout.title: The claim that gets pages pulled
callout.body: "Cures diabetes", "reverses arthritis", "guaranteed relief". These are the phrasings that attract regulatory attention and platform ad rejections. Rewrite as what the treatment involves and what patients report, sourced and attributed — never as an outcome you promise.

sections.h2: Malayalam, and the half of Trivandrum that never leaves Kerala
body: Behind the export economy is an ordinary city economy — hospitals and clinics, CBSE and state schools, tuition centres, jewellers, builders, restaurants, home services. For these, the export playbook is irrelevant and the local one is everything.

Kerala's literacy makes English usable across almost the whole market, so English-only sites limp along here in a way they wouldn't elsewhere. Limping isn't ranking. Malayalam script queries are real, romanised Malayalam is very common in typed search, and voice search in Malayalam is where a lot of "near me" intent now lives.

The efficient move is targeted, not total: a Google Business Profile filled out properly with Malayalam posts and replies, area pages using the names people actually search — Kazhakkoottam, Pattom, Vazhuthacaud, Kowdiar, Sreekaryam — and Malayalam versions of the handful of pages carrying real commercial intent. Not a mirrored site nobody updates.

sections.h2: Government-adjacent clients and the approval-cycle tax
body: Thiruvananthapuram is Kerala's capital, so a meaningful share of local organisations are state PSUs, government-linked institutions, cooperatives or bodies with a board that signs off on public communication. If that's you, the constraint on your SEO isn't budget. It's turnaround.

A private client approves a page in two days. A government-adjacent client approves it in four to eight weeks, and the version that comes back has been edited by three people who don't share a view. Content velocity collapses, and with it the timeline for results.

We plan around it. Technical work first, because it needs no copy approval and often produces the earliest gains. Batched approvals instead of trickled ones. Template-level sign-off so each new page in a family doesn't restart the process. And an honest timeline in the proposal — if approvals take six weeks, the 90-day guarantee is scoped against what can realistically ship in 90 days, and we say so before you sign.

callout.title: What we guarantee, stated properly
callout.body: We freeze your trailing-90-day qualified leads from organic search on day one. If we haven't beaten that number in 90 days, we keep working free until we do. We never promise a specific ranking position for a specific keyword, because nobody controls Google's index. SEO from ₹75,000/mo, smaller sites from ₹40,000/mo, ex-GST — see [pricing](/pricing).

faqs.q: Can one agency handle both a Technopark IT client and an Ayurveda resort?
faqs.a: Yes, but not with one plan. They share almost no keywords, no seasonality and no buyer psychology. We scope them as separate campaigns with separate baselines and separate reporting, even when the retainer is one invoice.

faqs.q: How much does SEO cost in Trivandrum?
faqs.a: Local agencies commonly quote ₹10,000–₹35,000 a month. That range typically buys one person's part-time attention. We start at ₹40,000 for smaller sites and ₹75,000 for a full retainer, ex-GST, month-to-month after the first quarter with 30 days' notice.

faqs.q: How far ahead should an Ayurveda centre publish seasonal content?
faqs.a: Aim for six months ahead of the season you sell into, minimum. A page needs time to be crawled, indexed and to accumulate signals before demand arrives. Publishing monsoon-treatment content in July means competing for this year's traffic with a page Google has just met.

faqs.q: What can't I say on an Ayurveda or medical website in India?
faqs.a: You can't advertise claims to diagnose, cure or prevent the conditions listed in the schedule of the Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act, 1954, and separate rules govern how registered practitioners may advertise. Describe the treatment, the qualifications and the process instead of promising outcomes, and have a lawyer review commercial pages.

faqs.q: Do Technopark companies need Malayalam SEO?
faqs.a: For selling, almost never — their buyers are in the US and Europe. For hiring, sometimes, and a careers section that ranks locally is genuinely valuable in a competitive talent market. Keep the two objectives on separate parts of the site so neither dilutes the other.
